prompt.context: A friend is considering purchasing a yoga studio that she is a member of. The yoga studio is located in the upper west side of Manhattan. The yoga studio is small and has a community-like environment that customers love. Currently, there are 10 teachers each teaching 2-4 classes/week, with a total of 100 classes/month offered by the yoga studio. The current owner has run the yoga studio for 5 years and recently the business suffered a loss. The lease ends at the end of the month, making it an appropriate time for the friend to acquire this yoga studio.
prompt.question: What are the key factors that the friend should be considering when deciding whether to acquire this yoga studio?

clarifying_info.a: Cost has been consistent; revenue has gone down by $48,000 between 2010 and 2011.

clarifying_info.q: What is the total monthly cost?

clarifying_info.a: Currently there are 100 classes per month.

clarifying_info.q: What is the charge per student per class?

exhibits.title: Breakeven Point – 2011 Data
exhibits.shows: Data table or exhibit presenting the 2011 financials used to calculate the breakeven number of students per class
exhibits.data: 100 classes/month; $10/student/class; total monthly cost $8,000; 2011 annual loss $24,000

exhibits.title: Enrollment Increase to Breakeven
exhibits.shows: Data or exhibit presenting the 2011 enrollment figures used to calculate the required percentage increase in enrollment to reach breakeven

framework: External: Yoga industry trends and market growth potential
External: Competitive landscape – number and proximity of competing yoga studios in the upper west side
Internal – Revenue: Number of classes (100/month) x students per class x price per student
Internal – Revenue drivers: maximum class capacity (20 students), current capacity utilization, pricing strategy
Internal – Cost: Teacher salaries (10 teachers, 2-4 classes/week), lease cost, maintenance/overhead
Profitability assessment: current loss, breakeven enrollment, path to profitability
Acquisition considerations: purchase price from current owner, switching costs for members with annual passes, upside scenario

questions.prompt: Q2a: If the studio offers 100 classes/month and charges $10/student, what is the breakeven number of students per class?
questions.guidance: Set revenue equal to monthly cost. Revenue = 100 classes x $10/student x N students/class = 1,000N. Set equal to $8,000 cost to solve for N.

math.setup: Revenue = Cost; 100 classes x $10/student x N students/class = $8,000

questions.prompt: Q2b: In 2011 the studio had a loss of $24,000. What was the average enrollment per class, and by what percentage does enrollment need to increase to break even?
questions.guidance: Convert annual loss to monthly loss, derive monthly revenue, then find students/class. Then calculate the percentage increase from current to breakeven enrollment.

math.setup: Monthly loss = $24,000 / 12 = $2,000; Monthly revenue = $8,000 - $2,000 = $6,000; $6,000 = 100 classes x $10/student x N; Enrollment increase = (8 - 6) / 6
math.answer: Average enrollment is 6 students/class; enrollment must increase by 33% to break even

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should the friend consider beyond the financial breakeven analysis before deciding whether to acquire the yoga studio?

categories.name: Market & Competition
ideas: Number of competing yoga studios in the upper west side
Differentiation of this studio's community environment
Barriers to entry for new competitors

categories.name: Acquisition Economics
ideas: Purchase price the current owner is asking
Negotiating leverage given the imminent lease expiration

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Ability to renegotiate or renew the lease on favorable terms
Class schedule optimization to improve utilization
Marketing spend needed to grow enrollment

categories.name: Customer & Revenue
ideas: Proportion of members on annual passes (switching costs)
Member loyalty and likelihood of churn under new ownership
Pricing elasticity – can price be raised above $10
Potential new revenue streams (workshops, retail, private sessions)

categories.name: Personal Fit
ideas: Friend's operational experience running a small business
Alignment with friend's financial goals and risk tolerance

recommendation: Do NOT acquire the yoga studio, especially if seeking short-term profit
To merely break even, enrollment must increase by 33% per class, which is a steep target in a competitive, community-based market in a short time horizon
risks: High switching costs if existing members have pre-purchased annual passes, limiting revenue recovery
Additional fixed acquisition cost (purchase price) makes profitability even harder to achieve
Competitive density of yoga studios on the upper west side constrains enrollment growth
next_steps: Obtain the asking purchase price from the current owner to quantify total investment required
Survey current members to assess retention likelihood under new ownership
Conduct competitive analysis of nearby studios to gauge realistic enrollment growth ceiling
If still interested, negotiate a lower acquisition price given the ongoing losses and expiring lease
